The pipeline proceeds in two stages: (1) a cold-start initialization using debiasing object-centric prompts to anchor motion inference in 2D visual evidence; and (2) a recursive logit-ranking mechanism that enforces statistical parity by using the median logit value as a dynamic threshold. Experimental evaluation across frontier VLMs on standard benchmarks demonstrates that SKR-ID significantly mitigates systematic biases. Our method improves open-source VLMs' Macro-F1 scores from 35.0-45.4% to 53.7-58.0%, without using any annotated data. These results show that SKR-ID can effectively improve 3D reasoning performance from a severely collapsed baseline. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/astudentuser/Codes_of_SKR-ID.

item.title: Complementarity-Driven Dual-Teacher Hierarchical Alignment for Zero-Shot EEG-to-Image Retrieval
item.description:
Relevance: 30% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Lukun Wu, Jie Li, Ziqi Ren, Ruiyang Xia, Yan Gao, Xinbo Gao
arXiv:2611.12798v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Decoding visual information from EEG is central to brain--computer interfaces and brain-inspired intelligence, and contrastive alignment with pretrained vision foundation models (VFMs) has become the dominant paradigm. However, existing methods align EEG solely with CLIP-family VFMs, leaving hierarchical visual information in neural responses under-exploited. To address this gap, we formulate a mechanism-paradigm correspondence view linking hierarchical visual processing (from appearance to semantics) to the complementary biases of cross-paradigm VFMs, with image-only models (e.g., DINO) and image--text models (e.g., CLIP) capturing distinct facets of this hierarchy. Guided by this view, we propose the Dual-Teacher Hierarchical Alignment (DTHA) framework. Concretely, a shared EEG encoder is supervised by frozen multi-blur CLIP and shallow DINOv2 teachers via dual-branch contrastive alignment, so each branch fully supervises the visual cues it emphasizes. A fused-retrieval objective learns adaptive weights to combine their complementary visual representations for zero-shot EEG-to-image retrieval. For the shared EEG encoder, we introduce the Attentive Modulated Scalp-Pattern Bank Encoder (AMSPBE), combining temporo-spatial attention with a learnable scalp-pattern bank for accurate, interpretable visual feature extraction, while modeling regional temporal dynamics and filter-bank topographies. On THINGS-EEG zero-shot retrieval, DTHA achieves 92.4% Top-1 accuracy, exceeding prior state of the art by 12.4 percentage points. Spatial, spectral, and representational-similarity analyses, together with THINGS-MEG evaluation, validate DTHA's effectiveness, biological plausibility, and cross-modality generalization. This complementarity-driven perspective shows that supervision from cross-paradigm VFMs enables more complete extraction of hierarchical visual information from brain activity.

item.title: AI-Generated Images as Data Source: The Dawn of Synthetic Era
item.description:
Relevance: 30% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Zuhao Yang, Yu Wei, Fangneng Zhan, Kunhao Liu, Muyu Xu, Xiaoqin Zhang, Ling Shao, Shijian Lu
arXiv:2310.01830v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The advancement of visual intelligence is intrinsically tethered to the availability of large-scale data. In parallel, generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) has unlocked the potential to create synthetic images that closely resemble real-world photographs. This prompts a compelling inquiry: how much visual intelligence could benefit from the advance of generative AI? This paper explores the innovative concept of harnessing these AI-generated images as new data sources, reshaping traditional modeling paradigms in visual intelligence. In contrast to real data, AI-generated data exhibit remarkable advantages, including unmatched abundance and scalability, the rapid generation of vast datasets, and the effortless simulation of edge cases. Built on the success of generative AI models, we examine the potential of their generated data in a range of applications, from training machine learning models to simulating scenarios for computational modeling, testing, and validation. We probe the technological foundations that support this groundbreaking use of generative AI, engaging in an in-depth discussion on the ethical, legal, and practical considerations that accompany this transformative paradigm shift. Through an exhaustive survey of current technologies and applications, this paper presents a comprehensive view of the synthetic era in visual intelligence. A project associated with this paper can be found at https://github.com/mwxely/AIGS .

item.title: InfCoiL: Coordinated Planner-Controller Learning for Closed-Loop Physics-Based Human-Object Interaction
item.description:
Relevance: 30% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Yude Zou, Yifei Yao, Yiwei Hao, Hanqing Wang, Xing Gao
arXiv:2611.11517v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Text- and goal-conditioned human-object interaction (HOI) provides an intuitive interface for specifying high-level intents in physics-based character animation. Mapping such intents to physically plausible, contact-rich behaviors naturally calls for a generative planner and a physics-based controller, yet existing planner-controller systems either execute plans open-loop or close the loop while keeping the planner fixed, so execution feedback never reshapes what is planned. We present InfCoiL, a closed-loop framework for physics-based HOI from coordinated planner-controller learning. InfCoiL couples a morphology-aware flow-matching planner with a unified multi-morphology controller through a shared morphology interface in an autoregressive plan-and-execute loop, and alternately fine-tunes both components with reinforcement learning from the same physical rollouts. To optimize the flow-matching planner online, we introduce Semantic Flow Policy Optimization (SFPO), which stochasticizes selected denoising transitions with channel-wise semantic covariance over heterogeneous HOI features and assigns group-relative, sequence-level rewards from complete closed-loop executions. On held-out OMOMO sequences, InfCoiL outperforms open-loop hierarchical baselines in goal-reaching task success and physical tracking accuracy. Project page: https://infcoil.github.io/

item.title: HumanSightBench: A Benchmark for Human Visual Perception in MLLMs
item.description:
Relevance: 30% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Zixin Su, Yangguang Lin, Zegang Peng, Yuntong Sun, Xuanyi Wang, Jiahao Wang, Qiankai Xu, Bing Yuan, Jinze Bai, Youbin Wu, Jingjia Huang, Ruyang Liu, Yanxu Hu
arXiv:2611.12305v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have demonstrated strong performance on knowledge-intensive and reasoning-based vision-language benchmark datasets, but still struggle to solve the visual questions that people can solve easily. Evaluating the differences between MLLMs and human-level visual perception is challenging due to end-to-end evaluation which combines various skills, or because we are uncertain if individual items are valid. Specifically, observed errors may reflect visual perception, language priors, background knowledge, question ambiguity, and underspecified answers. Our guideline for HumanSightBench is that we construct items that are human-easy by construction and model-hard by evaluation. HumanSightBench contains 2,876 visual questions with short answers across 7 top-level perceptual categories and 21 subcategories. We only include items that pass five inclusion gates: question clarity, answer uniqueness, visual grounding, human solvability, and text-only shortcut filtering. According to the protocol, errors are defined as incorrect answers on human-validated visual tasks with the evaluated interface. The inclusion gates are intended to reduce confounds from ambiguity and external knowledge. The best pass@3 score is 65.6% across eight evaluated MLLMs. No evaluated model exceeds 27.5% on Counting. These results identify capability gaps that are hidden by overall scores and can help future training experiments and held-out evaluation.

item.title: Locating and Repairing Domain Shift in VLM Trajectory Planning
item.description:
Relevance: 30% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Zhihong Cui, Hengyu Liu, Michael Alexander Riegler, Guandong Xu, Amir Taherkordi, Tor Skeie
arXiv:2611.10720v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are increasingly adopted as end-to-end driving planners, yet they suffer from cross-city domain shift. Existing methods treat this shift as a single quantity addressed by uniform alignment or single-site editing. We challenge this view on two counts: (i) domain shift in VLM trajectory planners is inherently structured across modality and layer, and (ii) a locate-then-repair recipe matched to this structure outperforms every uniform-objective baseline. We analyse domain shift via activation patching and uncover two regularities. (F1) Modality axis. Image and text tokens exhibit distinct shift patterns in each VLM. (F2) Layer axis. The layer-wise shift partition is architecture-dependent and dataset-stable. These findings recast domain shift as a two-dimensional tensor indexed by modality (image vs. text tokens) and layer, motivating a simple principle: locate where shift occurs, and repair only there. We instantiate this principle in MoLaRx (Modality-Layer Repair), a locate-then-repair framework. The Causal Importance Score (CIS) estimates the domain shift as a modality-layer tensor and partitions the layers into functional zones. CIS-Guided Selective Repair (CISR) then applies a matched operator (Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) / low-rank adaptation (LoRA) / freezing) to repair each zone, with the composition adapting automatically to each architecture. We evaluate MoLaRx on three architecturally distinct VLMs (LFM2-VL-1.6B, Qwen2-VL-2B, and PaliGemma2-3B) across two cross-city benchmarks (nuScenes and Argoverse 2). MoLaRx attains the lowest cross-city trajectory-error gap among adaptation methods in all six main-table settings, while using 50-60% fewer trainable parameters and 8.4-10.9 ms lower inference latency. In contrast, uniform MMD-only adaptation collapses in all six settings, highlighting the importance of structure-guided repair.

item.title: Virtual Task Prompting for Multi-Task Scene Understanding
item.description:
Relevance: 30% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Zedong Wang, Yucheng Wang, Dan Xu
arXiv:2611.11041v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-task scene understanding models typically rely on modified vision encoders or complex decoders for cross-task interaction, which limits their flexibility and compatibility with off-the-shelf vision foundation models (VFMs). We introduce Virtual Task Prompting (VTP), which frames multi-task prompting as retrieving task-adaptive compositions from a shared virtual state, where both the state and routing process are optimized in an end-to-end manner. Concretely, VTP maintains an expanded set of virtual tasks alongside the backbone. At each layer, learnable routing matrices read task-specific compositions as input to interact with image tokens and write the processed results back, forming explicit pathways that capture the intricacies among tasks outside the encoder. Since VTP keeps the backbone clean, it integrates seamlessly with pretrained VFMs, advancing the state of the art on Pascal-Context and NYUD-v2. Stress test on Taskonomy with 13 heterogeneous tasks further shows VTP's robustness in extreme settings. Ablations and analysis indicate that VTP's gains stem from adaptive routing rather than increased capacity. The project page is available at https://jacky1128.github.io/VTP/.

item.title: Heterogeneous Asymmetric Contrastive Distillation
item.description:
Relevance: 30% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Qi Wang, Jinjia Zhou
arXiv:2611.10672v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) between architectural families, e.g., from a Transformer teacher to a CNN student, is difficult because the two networks learn different representations. Logits share a label space, but heterogeneous teachers differ in logit offset, scale, and sharpness, and their non-target classes are less semantically organized. Conventional logit distillation matches these values sample by sample, asking the student to imitate how another architecture expresses its predictions. We argue that a heterogeneous teacher should pass on the relational structure of its predictions, i.e., how it arranges samples relative to one another, and propose Heterogeneous Asymmetric Contrastive Distillation (HACD) to transfer this structure. HACD maps teacher and student logits to centered, temperature-softened probability directions on a shared unit hypersphere, which removes architecture-dependent offsets and lets the temperature control how sharply peaked outputs enter the representation while keeping informative non-target classes. Each student output must then identify its own teacher target within the batch. Because every teacher target also acts as a negative for the others, HACD computes the targets on a moderately augmented view and contrasts both a moderate and a strong student view against them. HACD adds no learnable parameters and needs one teacher pass per sample. It achieves the best or second-best accuracy on 11 of 12 heterogeneous pairs on CIFAR-100, without ground-truth labels, and on 14 of 15 pairs on ImageNet-1K, improving over the reported vanilla KD results by 8.82 and 1.33 percentage points on average. Checkpoints are available at https://github.com/BTAEYANG/HACD-Heterogeneous-Asymmetric-Contrastive-Distillation; the code will be released upon publication.

item.title: AI has transformed maths — this is how we got here
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: Nature
Anil Ananthaswamy
Nature, Published online: 09 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03627-6 The story of how maths came to run the world, and created the artificial-intelligence models that might surpass human mathematicians.

item.title: ALAM: Algebraically Consistent Latent Action Model for Vision-Language-Action Models
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Zuojin Tang, Haoyun Liu, Xinyuan Chang, Changjie Wu, Dongjie Huo, Yandan Yang, Bin Liu, Zhejia Cai, Feng Xiong, Mu Xu, jiachen Luo, De Ma, Zhiheng Ma, Gang Pan
arXiv:2605.10819v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models remain constrained by the scarcity of action-labeled robot data, whereas action-free videos provide abundant evidence of how the physical world changes. Latent action models offer a promising way to extract such priors from videos, but reconstruction-trained latent codes are not necessarily suitable for policy generation: they may predict future observations while lacking the structure needed to be reused or generated coherently with robot actions. We introduce ALAM (Algebraic Latent Action Model), an Algebraically Consistent Latent Action Model that turns temporal relations in action-free video into structural supervision. Given frame triplets, ALAM learns latent transitions that are grounded by reconstruction while being regularized by composition and reversal consistency, encouraging a locally additive transition space. For downstream VLA learning, we freeze the pretrained encoder and use its latent transition sequences as auxiliary generative targets, co-generated with robot actions under a joint flow-matching objective. This couples structured latent transitions with flow-based policy generation, allowing the policy to exploit ALAM's locally consistent transition geometry without requiring latent-to-action decoding. Representation probes show that ALAM reduces additivity and reversibility errors by 25-85 times over unstructured latent-action baselines and improves long-horizon cumulative reconstruction. When transferred to VLA policies, ALAM raises the average success rate from 47.9% to 85.0% on MetaWorld MT50 and from 94.2% to 98.1% on LIBERO, with consistent gains on real-world manipulation tasks. Ablations further confirm that the strongest improvements arise from the synergy between algebraically structured latent transitions and joint flow matching. Our code is available at: https://github.com/Mark-zjtang/ALAM/tree/main.

item.title: Ask About the Right Moment: Training-Free Object Identity Reasoning for Video-Language Models
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Di Yang, Xiaochang Li, Muyang Liu, Yufei Wang, Yanhai Xiong
arXiv:2610.31471v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Many questions about a video concern one physical object. Where does the ball end up after the cups are shuffled? Which card is the queen? How often was the mug covered? Open video-language models (Video-LMs) recognise such objects in single frames but do not keep them apart over time. On shuffled shell games, open models from eight families stay near chance, and so do published tool agents. We separate semantic identity binding from temporal identity maintenance. Binding should happen at a moment when the evidence for the object is visible, and maintenance should be left to a tracker. Track, Then Bind implements this principle without training. A promptable video tracker follows every candidate object and draws it with a track number. A frozen vision-language model (VLM) answers one question about the identifying evidence, which binds the target to a track. The answer is then derived from a text description of the tracks. With Qwen3-VL-32B, the agent solves both VET-Bench tasks, where a fine-tuned trajectory model reaches 92% and 90%. On real cup games from the Perception Test, it raises accuracy from 35.5% to 52.3%. Without retuning, the same configuration also solves VET-Bench with Gemma 4 and GPT-5.5. Its track-derived visibility timelines add 8.8-17.9 points on TOC-Bench for open models. GPT-6.1 already answers 92.5% of the real cup games directly but 71.0% through our pipeline, while our timelines still raise its TOC-Bench accuracy from 52.5% to 57.7%. The benefit of external tracking thus depends on the underlying model and the task.

item.title: LAFP: Preserving Latent Action Structure in Latent Policy Learning via Flow Matching
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Jiexi Lyu, Xizhou Bu, Qingqiu Huang, Chufeng Tang, Xiaoshuai Hao, Hongbo Wang, Wei Li
arXiv:2606.10517v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Learning high quality latent actions from large-scale unlabeled videos, coupled with limited real-world interaction data for training an action decoder, has emerged as a promising paradigm for scalable latent policy learning. However, existing approaches typically rely on behavior cloning, which tends to collapse inherently multimodal action distributions into unimodal ones, thereby degrading the pretrained latent action structure. While flow matching provides a potential alternative, directly applying it leads to a misalignment between latent actions and physical actions during action decoder training, due to the stochastic nature of the learned policy. To address these, we propose Latent Action Flow Policy (LAFP), which leverages flow matching for latent policy learning and introduces an inference-time interpolation mechanism to mitigate stochasticity-induced misalignment. Experimental results demonstrate that LAFP consistently outperforms prior methods on most downstream imitation learning tasks, achieving an 8.2\% improvement in average success rate while incurring less than 1x additional inference overhead.

item.title: AutoVLA-D: Learn a Trajectory-Geometric Condition from Reasoning for Autonomous Driving VLA
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Yuguang Yang, Zhewen Tan, Canyu Chen, Linlin Yang, Cheng Chi, Chunyang Liu, Kehua Sheng, Jinyu Yang, Baochang Zhan, Bo Zhang, Yan Wang, Xianbin Cao
arXiv:2611.12382v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Autoregressive VLA planning usually predicts continuous trajectories as the final output, but driving instructions often describe actions rather than ego states, which weakens direct conditioning on the final continuous trajectory. We address this gap with TrajCond, which introduces a discrete trajectory-geometric condition for VLA planning. Specifically, we represent TrajCond as a 1D-Brohan differential action trajectory and learn it with a two-stage training framework before final continuous trajectory prediction. With the simultaneous autoregressive generation of discrete and numeric trajectories, we name our method AutoVLA-D (Double). Experiments on NAVSIM navtest, nuScenes, and NeuroNCAP show that discrete trajectories are weaker as direct outputs but more effective as TrajCond, consistently improving final continuous trajectory prediction across closed-loop and open-loop driving benchmarks. Code is available at https://github.com/ShivaTeam/AutoVLA-D.

item.title: Equilibrium Selection in Coordination Games with Planned Actions and Scouting
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: arXiv Economics
Wolfgang Kuhle
arXiv:2609.17608v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study Stag Hunt games in which every action requires planning and preparation. Before players act, they observe noisy signals of their opponent's preparations and can revise their plans, which allows players to screen for cooperation. As screening becomes more precise and cheap, small trembles ensure that, in every equilibrium, play yields the payoff-dominant outcome with a probability that converges to one, even when the safe, low payoff equilibrium is risk dominant. Across scenarios, we emphasize that decomposing an action into (i) preparation and (ii) execution allows us to analyze simultaneous-move games in which players partially observe each other's contemporaneous actions.

item.title: HSGNav: Hypothesis Scene Graphs for Multi-Scale Lifelong Navigation under Object Relocation
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Kaiyao Liao, Qingfeng Li, Chen Chen, Qing Sun, Ningbo Gu, Xiaoze Wu, Haochen Zhao, Ying Li, Jianwei Niu
arXiv:2611.10547v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In real homes, assistive robots must repeatedly locate targets from large furniture to tiny tabletop items, as people move objects between household surfaces. Uniformly instantiating detections at different scales as 3D objects can be brittle for small on-surface items; without explicit object-state validation, stale entries may persist after scene changes. Our key insight is to separate persistent 3D furniture entities from revisable surface-object hypotheses, retaining their visual evidence without requiring independent object geometry. We formalize this design as the Hypothesis Scene Graph (HSG), which preserves small-object evidence and supports local revision without rebuilding the stable entity topology. Building on HSG, HSGNav uses this separation for multi-scale lifelong navigation: retrieval selects entity or hypothesis evidence according to target scale, exploration acquires additional surface observations, and verification confirms target presence or invalidates contradicted hypothesis records. Because existing lifelong benchmarks such as GOAT-Bench rarely require mid-episode memory invalidation or multi-scale search, we introduce FAROS-Bench (Find And Re-find Objects across Scales) for mid-episode relocation of surface objects and multi-scale find goals. Experiments show that HSGNav performs competitively on GOAT-Bench while substantially outperforming prior methods on FAROS-Bench.

item.title: Shape-based Figure-Ground Organization in Vision Transformers
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Matthias Tangemann, Benjamin Lo, Zygmunt Pizlo, Kaleem Siddiqi, Dirk B. Walther, Sven Dickinson
arXiv:2607.08932v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Rich perceptual structure emerges in modern vision encoders. Several studies have shown that the internal representation in many vision transformers separates foreground objects from the background, however, little is known about the visual cues that have been learned by these models. In this work, we study whether figure-ground organization in a broad range of 25 vision transformers relies on generalizable shape cues, rather than on superficial texture statistics. To do so we train linear probes to classify patches as figure or ground, and evaluate them zero-shot on synthetic stimuli where individual cues are systematically manipulated. For a broad range of vision encoders, we find that probes are robust to the random replacement of textures in the input image, suggesting that the emerging figure-ground organization relies on shape cues. Probes also generalize in a zero-shot fashion to synthetic images where individual shape cues, recognizability and spatial priors are controlled for. Our experiments reveal a strong influence of surroundedness and convexity cues, while results for parallelism and symmetry are more nuanced. More detailed analyses reveal stronger evidence for shape-based cues in larger models, that models trained for object-recognition tend to be less robust to texture changes and that figure-ground information emerges most prominently in middle layers. Taken together, our study demonstrates that emerging figure-ground organization in recent vision encoders relies strongly on generalizable shape cues, advancing our understanding of the internal processing in vision transformers, and opening an exciting avenue for computational research on human visual perception. Code and data is available at https://github.com/mtangemann/mlvbench.

item.title: Prism: Bidirectional Self-Teaching for Unified Multimodal Models
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Peng Zhang, Qian Chen, Xianyin Zhang, Yimin Tian, Ruite Fei, Dongyi Lv, Lifan Guo, Chi Zhang, Shuai Liu
arXiv:2611.06343v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Unified Multimodal Models (UMMs) aim to support visual understanding and generation within a single model. Existing post-training methods either use understanding as a fixed teacher to improve generation, or rely on ground-truth trajectories to supervise both understanding and generation. Prism instead derives bidirectional supervision from self-generated interleaved rollouts, constructing training targets according to the reliability of their text and image chains. We propose Prism, a bidirectional self-teaching post-training method for UMMs. Like a prism decomposing mixed light, Prism decouples a coupled interleaved trajectory into a text chain and an image chain, assesses the reliability of each chain, and constructs a corresponding training target from their reliability states. Experiments on both SenseNova-U1 and BAGEL show that Prism improves both understanding and generation. On the generation side, GenEval improves from 85.8 to 89.2 (+3.4), and DPG improves from 86.1 to 87.3 (+1.2) on SenseNova-U1. On the understanding side, the total MME score improves from 2282.6 to 2311.6, and MMVP improves from 58.0 to 62.0. Consistent improvements are observed on BAGEL. These results highlight that Prism enables coordinated improvements in generation and understanding by constructing reliability-guided self-training targets from self-generated trajectories, without relying on an external verifier or externally annotated corrected trajectories during target construction. Code is available at https://github.com/aliyun/qwen-dianjin/tree/master/DianJin-Prism.

item.title: SurgWorld: Learning Surgical Representations Beyond Observation via Latent Prediction
item.description:
Relevance: 28% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Jingkun Yue, Pengxiang Wang, Siqi Zhang, Zinan Jia, Yiyao Zhang, Huihuan Xu, Yichang Hao, Xiaohong Liu, Zongbo Han, Guangyu Wang
arXiv:2611.11140v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Surgical procedures are inherently partially observable, requiring surgeons to continuously infer evolving anatomical dynamics and future surgical states beyond the current observation. However, existing self-supervised learning methods primarily learn from observed surgical videos through masked reconstruction or predicting representations within the camera's current field of view, lacking the capability to explicitly model the out-of-sight surgical dynamics. Inspired by latent predictive world models, we introduce SurgWorld, a video-native, self-supervised framework for surgical representation learning, which treats a specified spatial or temporal shift as a pseudo-action and learns to predict the target latent representation from a partial observation. Specifically, we propose Out-of-Sight Dynamics Modeling (OSDM) as the pretraining objective for predicting representations conditioned on relative spatio-temporal shifts. We further regularize the learned latent dynamics from OSDM with a Geometric Visual Similarity (GVS) objective by aligning patch-level relational structures between predicted and target representations, preserving spatial geometry and local visual coherence for dense perception. These two objectives are integrated through an agglomerative training framework that consolidates complementary supervisory signals from multiple teachers to learn a unified latent representation of surgical dynamics and visual geometry. Extensive transfer learning experiments on 17 surgical benchmarks show that SurgWorld consistently outperforms existing vision foundation models across surgical workflow recognition, fine-grained action understanding, and dense visual perception. We further conduct tailored qualitative and quantitative analyses, demonstrating that SurgWorld effectively captures surgical dynamics beyond the directly observed context through latent prediction.

item.title: Does Pose Encoding Matter? Analyzing Geometric Representations for Discrete Motion Vocabulary Learning
item.description:
Relevance: 28% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Amir Kimiyaie, Nahal Mafi, Hamed Tabkhi
arXiv:2611.11093v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Compressing continuous human motion into a finite vocabulary of discrete tokens is now the first stage of many motion understanding and generation pipelines. Vector quantization partitions a latent space into Voronoi cells around a finite codebook, but the geometry of that latent space is inherited from the input pose encoding, and it is unclear which encoding admits an efficient discretization. We study four encodings that place skeletal motion in different geometric spaces: Gaussian joint heatmaps on the pixel lattice, which we show to be a morphological dilation of the joint point set by a quadratic structuring function; root-relative joint positions in Euclidean space; local joint rotations on $\SO$ through a continuous 6D embedding; and a redundant full kinematic encoding. For each, we train VQ-VAE tokenizers whose codebooks lie on the unit hypersphere, varying codebook size, temporal stride, and code dimension. Beyond reconstruction, we measure codebook utilization and the effective vocabulary size, i.e., the number of equiprobable spherical Voronoi cells with the same entropy as the observed token distribution. Rotation and position encodings keep converting additional codewords into effective vocabulary, whereas the full kinematic encoding saturates at a few hundred effective cells and heatmaps at fewer than sixty. The smallest code dimension gives the highest utilization for three of the four encodings, and the effect of temporal stride depends on the encoding. Encodings of the same pose family can thus yield effective vocabularies differing by an order of magnitude, a difference that reconstruction loss alone does not reveal, which points to input geometry as a first-order design choice in motion tokenization.

item.title: These AI agents design your perfect robot-powered lab — and run it for you
item.description:

Nature, Published online: 06 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03587-x A team of artificial-intelligence agents simulates a laboratory of robots and instruments to ensure that the physical workspace functions smoothly and then directs that workspace’s operations.

item.title: PoEM: Predicting RL Outcomes from Existing Policies
item.description:
Relevance: 28% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Kimia Hamidieh, Giannis Daras, Antonio Torralba
arXiv:2609.30226v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Foundation models are post-trained with reinforcement learning (RL) to maximize specific rewards, such as helpfulness, correctness, or instruction following. This post-training process is computationally intensive, sometimes unstable, and has to be run from scratch every time the reward model changes or when we want to combine multiple rewards. We hence ask: given a new reward function, is it possible to predict the policy RL would produce without actually training on that reward? We answer this in the affirmative by introducing PoEM, a framework for predicting RL outcomes using models previously trained on other rewards. First, we build on the fact that if the new reward function can be written as a linear combination of existing ones, then the optimal policy can be expressed as a combination of the existing policies in log-probability space. Surprisingly, even in cases where the rewards are not linearly connected, we observe that policies learned through RL often span an approximately low-rank subspace across rewards. To our benefit, the weights for this combination can be estimated using only the reward or basis policy outputs on the samples. We turn these observations into an algorithm that takes post-trained models and a target reward function, and approximates the target RL policy without any additional RL training. We experimentally evaluate our approach across programmatic and learned rewards for open-ended generation, with additional experiments on math reasoning, tool calling, and image generation.

item.title: Split and Bridge: Multimodal Generation via Diffusion Bridging
item.description:
Relevance: 28% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Ahmad Arrabi, Xiaohan Zhang, Xingyu Li, Safwan Wshah
arXiv:2611.10441v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Visual data are often expressed through multiple complementary modalities (e.g., images and segmentation masks), each capturing different aspects of the same underlying structure. Most existing multimodal methods adopt a top-down paradigm, learning a shared latent variable through joint training from scratch, which limits scalability. We propose Split and Bridge (SnB), a bottom-up framework for multimodal generation that couples pretrained unimodal diffusion models at sampling time. Rather than learning a unified latent space, SnB generates coherent multimodal samples by following a shared diffusion trajectory up to a split point and then branching into modality-specific trajectories guided by a bridge module. This design enables plug-and-play reuse of powerful pretrained models without joint training, making it scalable and easily adaptable. Across standard benchmarks (PolyMNIST, CelebAMask-HQ) and more complex settings (PIE-Bench++, ROCO), SnB achieves a strong balance between sample quality and coherence. We show that SnB naturally extends to downstream zero-shot tasks such as interleaved co-generation, image editing, and style coupling/decoupling. Our results demonstrate that bottom-up generation provides a practical framework that complements existing top-down multimodal approaches. Code is available at https://github.com/AhmadArrabi/SnB

item.title: Transferable reconstruction of equilibria in network dynamics from sentinel nodes
item.description:
Relevance: 28% | Source: arXiv Physics and Society
Naoki Masuda, Bisna Mary Eldo, Tharusha Bandara
arXiv:2609.27968v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Reconstructing the state of a large networked system from measurements at only a few nodes is a challenge for monitoring, prediction, and intervention. Here we ask whether such reconstruction is possible for equilibrium states and whether it can transfer across different nonlinear dynamics. We study this question across various networks and across $17$ nonlinear dynamics on networks from different domains. For each network, we observe only a vanishingly small fraction of sentinel nodes and train either a neural network or linear decoder. We find that accurate reconstruction is often possible, and that transferability is structured rather than universal. Eleven dynamics with adjacency-matrix-type coupling form a robust transferable class. By contrast, six diffusively coupled dynamics form isolated transfer components. Non-random sentinel selection is consistently important, and linear decoders often approach neural-network performance. These results show that sparse node observations can encode enough information to reconstruct full network equilibria across broad families of nonlinear dynamics, while also revealing sharp limits to universal transfer.

item.title: OCEAN: A Five-Phase Framework for Meaningful Change
item.description:
Relevance: 28% | Source: arXiv Physics and Society
A. Fronzetti Colladon
arXiv:2611.12803v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Managing meaningful change requires more than motivation, insight, or isolated techniques. This paper introduces OCEAN, a five-phase conceptual framework for structuring nonclinical developmental conversations and change-oriented work in coaching and in the practice of leaders and HR professionals. The five phases are Observe, Create, Expose, Awaken, and Nurture. In Observe, individuals develop a systemic, present-oriented understanding of the situation. In Create, they turn that understanding into goals that are meaningful and actionable. In Expose, they identify the attempted solutions that maintain the difficulty they are meant to remove, along with the resistances, biases, and self-deceptions that keep them in place. In Awaken, they activate new behaviors through planning, reframing, paradoxical movement, and emotionally significant experiences. In Nurture, they consolidate progress through repetition, habits, connection, and sustainable contexts. OCEAN integrates insights from systemic and interactional thinking, goal construction, emotional awareness, and habit consolidation into a structured process.

item.title: Representation Learning for 3D Brain Imaging: A Benchmark
item.description:
Relevance: 28% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Pierre Falconnier (MYRIAD), Robin Trombetta (MYRIAD), Nicolas Duchateau (MYRIAD), Carole Lartizien (MYRIAD)
arXiv:2611.10007v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many deep learning architectures for computer vision tasks rely on features extracted by a pre-trained encoder on large databases of natural 2D RGB images. However, the wide domain gap with medical images hampers the direct transfer of optimized deep learning models from computer vision to clinical applications. Recently, self-supervised pre-training and foundation models emerged as promising alternatives to mitigate these limitations. Yet, constructing such models for medical imaging faces critical challenges, including designing and adapting training strategies for large 3D volume datasets, and the need for standardized benchmarks to evaluate feature extraction performance. In this study, we propose an extensive comparison of vision encoders with a focus on 3D brain MRI. First, we consider 8 fully and self-supervised models pretrained on natural images (e.g. ResNet, DINO, CLIP) and 10 backbone architectures trained on medical images, either based on supervised (e.g. RadImageNet) or self-supervised (e.g. BiomedCLIP, SimCLR) tasks. All pre-trained encoders are evaluated on various downstream tasks to assess the representation power of their latent representations, including age and sex prediction as well as disease classification on the ADNI and PPMI datasets. Our study shows that 2D encoders pre-trained on natural images perform the most favorably, even compared to models pre-trained on more than 100k brain MRI volumes, highlighting the need for more suitable and robust methods for representation learning in 3D medical imaging. The source code for this study is publicly available at: https: //github.com/PierreFalconnier/brain-representation-benchmark.

item.title: Beyond Head Importance: Collective Computation in Video Transformers
item.description:
Relevance: 27% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Yi Yang, Siyuan Liu, Bingbing Nie
arXiv:2611.11875v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Attention heads in video Transformers vary greatly in functional importance. Understanding their contributions requires examining not only which heads are important, but also how they participate in collective computation within the network. We study this collective computation from two perspectives: the downstream use of head outputs and the composition of interactions across layers. Ablation analyses of four video Transformers show that high-importance heads identified on a single task also support other video understanding tasks and help preserve the representational structure that distinguishes different videos. Representational responses to head ablation correlate weakly with head importance after the attention module, but more strongly after the MLP in the same block. Adapting this downstream processing through MLP-only fine-tuning further improves the use of lower-importance head outputs. Meanwhile, through composition across layers, sets of heads with shorter spatiotemporal attention distances support stronger perturbation responses at distant tokens than sets with longer distances. Their joint ablation causes even greater performance loss than ablating equally sized sets of high-importance heads, revealing collective contributions not fully captured by individual importance rankings. These findings highlight collective computation as a key perspective for understanding attention head function: functional contributions depend on both how head outputs are used downstream and how local interactions compose across layers.

item.title: UNIVERS: Learning UNIversal Voxel-wise Embedding via Randomized Synthesis for generalizable one-shot landmark localization
item.description:
Relevance: 27% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Derong Yu, Qingsong Zhao, Yanbing Yue, Yikai Li, Zhi Zhang, Guoyan Zheng
arXiv:2610.29098v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: One-shot landmark localization in volume scans with varying fields of view (FOVs) is challenging. While existing self-supervised learning methods have shown promising performance, they rely on contrastive learning built upon augmented views of the same image, which inherently limits their generalization in cross-modality scenarios. This motivates research on cross-modality embedding learning using paired multi-modality images. However, existing methods suffer from not only limited training data, but also the requirement of multi-stage iterative training. To address these limitations, we propose UNIVERS, an end-to-end trainable framework that learns UNIversal Voxel-wise Embedding via Randomized Synthesis. Our framework leverages diverse pseudo-data synthesized from organ shape templates, with randomization applied to semantic layout, visual appearance, FOV, and spatial pose. Coupled with cross-domain discriminative voxel-wise contrastive learning, this domain randomization strategy forces the network to disregard domain-specific biases and learn features that are robust against variations in imaging contrast, resolution, and spatial context. Consequently, the trained model enables one-shot landmark localization in multi-modality volume scans with arbitrary FOVs. In this study, the efficacy of the proposed method is demonstrated by applying it to the task of localizing the adrenal glands, which are paired, small, and irregular endocrine organs. In particular, comprehensive experiments are conducted on three challenging adrenal gland datasets. The experimental results demonstrate that UNIVERS consistently outperforms the state-of-the-art (SOTA) one-shot landmark localization approaches, with particularly prominent advantages in cross-modality scenarios. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/Kendra9999/UNIVERS.

item.title: WanderBench: Can World Models Explore Dynamic Worlds from Video?
item.description:
Relevance: 27% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Yuhang Chen, Jiheng Li, Jiale Wang, Zai Wang, Guangyue Liu
arXiv:2611.12557v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Video world models conditioned on an input video make it possible to explore real, recorded dynamic scenes, enabling re-shooting of footage, free-viewpoint replay, and real-to-sim environments for embodied agents. Such uses require the generated rollout to stay faithful to the recorded world, yet existing benchmarks start from a single image or a text prompt, and video-conditioned generation is evaluated mainly on perceptual quality and camera following. These evaluations do not directly assess whether exploration preserves subject identity, event progression, and scene consistency upon revisiting a location. We introduce WanderBench, a benchmark for exploring dynamic worlds from video. It comprises 745 single-shot source videos of real and AI-generated content in three difficulty tiers (3-25 s), paired with camera routes given as keyboard actions, and evaluates six dimensions with 24 human-validated sub-metrics. Benchmarking eight models, we find that as clips grow longer, models keep the static scene and visual quality but lose camera control and the source dynamics, and that none keeps revisited places consistent. We further propose WanderLand, a training-free framework that conditions each frame of a frozen model on the same-instant source and, on revisits, on its own earlier static content. WanderLand improves five models on every dimension, by up to 8.3 points in source-dynamics fidelity.

item.title: Advancing AI Capabilities and Evolving Labor Outcomes
item.description:
Relevance: 27% | Source: arXiv Economics
Jacob Dominski, Tyler Boes, Yong Suk Lee
arXiv:2507.08244v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper examines how labor market outcomes have evolved across occupations as AI capabilities advanced from generative AI chatbots to reasoning models and AI agents. We construct an occupational AI exposure score that measures the share of each occupation's work that AI could perform at each capability stage, and link the change in exposure to the Current Population Survey from January 2023 through June 2026, using first-difference and fixed-effects designs at the occupation and individual level, with 2017 to 2022 as a placebo period. We find that occupations with larger increases in exposure show no change in employment or unemployment relative to occupations with comparable workforces. However, the composition of the workforce in these occupations changed. The number of workers under 30 decreased by about 8 percent per standard deviation of the change in exposure, and the decline is concentrated among workers without a college degree and builds gradually from 2023. It is not accompanied by higher unemployment among young workers who were already in these occupations, which suggests a decline in entry rather than an increase in exit. The decline is smaller when remote work is held fixed, but it remains. On the other hand, college graduates aged 30 to 49 gained full-time employment. Part-time work declined, weekly hours increased slightly, and the workforce in these occupations became older and more educated. In sum, the early effects of AI appear in the composition of the workforce rather than in the number of jobs.

Shamini Bundell, Nick Petrić Howe
Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03582-2 Genomes from thousands of ancient individuals show how migrations helped shape Celtic and Germanic languages — plus, how the brain may regulate emotions differently than we thought.

item.title: Disentangling Channel Semantics in Vision Transformers via Token Decorrelation and Composition-Aware Modulation
item.description:
Relevance: 27% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Daeun Kim, Hyesong Choi, Hyejin Park, Dongbo Min
arXiv:2611.10497v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-channel images encode heterogeneous channel semantics aligned over a shared spatial structure, which requires models to jointly capture globally shared structure and channel-specific variations. Recent multi-channel Vision Transformers attempt to address this challenge by augmenting the [CLS] token with memory tokens to organize multi-channel representations under varying channel compositions. However, we find that these context tokens collapse onto a few dominant channels under high inter-channel redundancy, producing redundant representations and a biased global summary that fails to reliably support composition-aware channel interpretation. We propose MuCa-ViT (Multi-Channel Composition-Aware Vision Transformer), a unified framework that addresses these limitations through two coupled mechanisms. Factorial Token Learning (FTL) enforces token-level decorrelation among context tokens, encouraging the [CLS] token to capture globally shared semantics while memory tokens preserve complementary channel-specific cues. Channel Composition-Aware Modulation (CAM) uses the FTL-refined [CLS] as a semantic anchor to generate sample-wise modulation signals, which enable composition-aware interpretation of channels within a unified backbone rather than relying on static channel embeddings. Experiments on JUMP-CP, CHAMMI, and So2Sat show that MuCa-ViT outperforms prior multi-channel ViTs across all three benchmarks, and the magnitude of improvement aligns with the inter-channel redundancy of each dataset ($\rho \in [0.19, 0.77]$), validating the diagnostic analysis that motivates our design. Our code is available at https://github.com/kimdanni/MuCa-ViT .

item.title: Tiny Evidence Region Localization with Selective Contrastive On-Policy Self-Distillation
item.description:
Relevance: 27% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Yujuan Pang, Wenhao Xu, Yinglei Teng
arXiv:2611.10734v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multimodal large language models have made progress in general visual tasks. However, limitations remain in fine-grained visual tasks requiring evidence from minute image regions. Existing methods primarily train models using evidence-related regions while overlooking the influence of extensive background regions, resulting in a limited ability to resist interference from irrelevant regions. We propose selective positive-negative on-policy self-distillation (SPN-OPSD), which considers both evidence and background regions. Supervision from both views improves the model's ability to resist interference from irrelevant regions. Furthermore, selective token-level distillation provides more informative supervision, improving the model's ability to attend to evidence regions in Fine-Grained Visual Tasks. On Qwen3.5-2B, SPN-OPSD improves accuracy on V* Bench, ZoomBench, and MME-RealWorld-Lite from 76.44%, 45.92%, and 57.43% to 84.82%, 54.56%, and 59.56%, respectively. Similar gains are also observed on Qwen3.5-0.8B.

item.title: Reaching Is Not Finding: Map-Anchored Visual Prompting for the Last Mile of Aerial Vision-Language Navigation
item.description:
Relevance: 27% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Ningbo Li, Kebin Liu, Jingcan Chen, Weichen Zhang, Rong Ding, Yunhao Liu, Mo Li
arXiv:2611.11510v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Aerial vision-language navigation (VLN) asks a drone to find an object described in natural language. The description usually locates the object relative to named landmarks, such as streets and buildings. We observe that current navigators often bring the drone close to the target and then stop at the wrong place: they reach the target without finding it. This gap is shared by navigators of very different designs, from imitation learners to a fine-tuned 7B vision-language model. A simple test reveals the cause. When we replace the target object in the instruction with another one next to the same landmarks, no navigator goes to it, and most stop where they did before. Navigators learn to reach the landmarks, not to identify the described object. We therefore propose MAP-VP, a plug-and-play module for the last step. After any navigator stops, MAP-VP draws the landmarks named in the instruction onto the drone's current view, using the landmark outlines that the benchmark provides on a map. A fine-tuned 4B vision-language model then locates the target relative to these landmarks. The training data are generated automatically from the benchmark annotations. Neither drawing the landmarks nor fine-tuning helps much alone, but together they are highly effective. Without retraining any navigator, MAP-VP significantly improves all six navigators we test on CityNav. It roughly doubles the success rate of the two strongest trained navigators, raising HETT from 25.9% to 54.6% and FlightGPT from 24.2% to 48.9%, whereas CityNav's official detector-based last step adds less than two points to HETT.

item.title: Training Vision Transformers to Focus: Emergence of Spatial Attention Head Specialization
item.description:
Relevance: 27% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Yuji Nozawa, Yu-Chieh Lin, Youyang Ng
arXiv:2611.11890v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Self-supervised learning in Vision Transformer models, such as DINO, enables robust visual perception without requiring labeled data by leveraging large-scale image datasets. However, these models lack a focusing mechanism during training, resulting in perceptual representations that are often ambiguous or overly similar. In this work, we introduce two visual focusing loss functions designed to establish correspondence between the model's attention and specific regions within images. Specifically, we leverage the multi-head attention mechanism within the model to selectively steer the model's focus, leading to the emergence of spatial attention head specialization, characterized by diverse and spatially focused perceptual capabilities without requiring annotations. Through both qualitative and quantitative evaluations, we demonstrate that our method substantially increases the spatial selectivity and diversity of attention heads, improving both interpretability and performance on dense prediction tasks such as zero-shot image segmentation.

item.title: Evolutionary games on networks with negative edge-based environmental feedback
item.description:
Relevance: 27% | Source: arXiv Physics and Society
Katherine Betz, Feng Fu, Naoki Masuda
arXiv:2611.11029v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Environmental feedback can fundamentally alter the game payoff structure underlying the evolution of cooperation. How feedback-evolving games interact with population structure under non-weak selection remains incompletely understood. We study an evolutionary game on networks in which each edge has a binary environmental state that determines the payoff matrix used by the two connected individuals. By assumption, cooperation tends to improve the local environment, which in turn favors defection, thereby creating negative feedback between strategies coupled with the environmental condition. We analyze the model under strong selection using a mean-field approximation, a pair approximation that tracks both strategy pairs and edge environments, and agent-based simulations. In well-mixed populations, the feedback can generate bistability between full cooperation and full defection, as well as sustained oscillations arising through a Hopf bifurcation. Sparse networks (i.e., with low nodes' degrees) can eliminate bistability, suppress oscillations, and produce stable intermediate levels of cooperation. The pair approximation captures these effects and generally agrees more closely with simulations on sparse networks than the mean-field approximation. Our results show that edge-based environmental feedback and network structure, such as density of edges, interact to determine whether the fraction of cooperators stabilizes or oscillates over time.

item.title: Tac-DINO: Learning Tactile Features with Patch Alignment
item.description:
Relevance: 27% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Hong Li, Yankang Dong, Yue Xu, Yihan Tang, Jiamin Qiu, Qihang Yao, Xing Zhu, Yujun Shen, Nan Xue, Yong-Lu Li
arXiv:2606.12069v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Multisensory perception is essential for robotic manipulation, with tactile sensing providing critical information for fine-grained, contact-rich interactions. Although prior work integrates tactile and spatial signals to improve perception, vision-tactile learning commonly relies on object-level alignment. Addressing this limitation requires systematically aligned 3D vision-tactile data. We develop a data collection system and introduce Touch3D, a dataset comprising 505 real-world objects and 20,025 tactile contacts. Building on this dataset, we establish the Contact-Centric Multimodal Tactile Representation Benchmark (CoMT-Bench), which expands evaluation from object-level retrieval and tactile properties to include patch-level contact evaluation. We further propose Geometry-Relation Distilled Tactile-Centric Cross-Modal Learning (GeoTAC), which explores tactile learning across all multisensory data. In experiments on the Touch3D test set, patch-level alignment improves the average score by 5.32 over object-level alignment, with GeoTAC's geometric supervision improving it by a further 4.48. In robotic manipulation, GeoTAC improves TP by 19.14 and 11.34 over DINOv2 (Vision-only) and DINOv2 (Vision-Tactile), respectively. Project page: https://lihongcs.github.io/tacdino.

item.title: How the brain protects itself from Parkinson’s disease

Sarah DeWeerdt
Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03171-3 Brains are resilient. Harnessing their self-protective mechanisms might help to prevent or slow the progression of this neurodegenerative condition.

item.title: LINE: LLM-based Iterative Neuron Explanations for Vision Models
item.description:
Relevance: 27% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Vladimir Zaigrajew, Micha{\l} Piechota, Gaspar Sekula, Pawe{\l} Gelar, Przemys{\l}aw Biecek
arXiv:2604.08039v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Interpreting the concepts encoded by individual neurons in deep neural networks is a crucial step towards understanding their complex decision-making processes and ensuring AI safety. Despite recent progress in neuron labeling, existing methods often limit the search space to predefined concept vocabularies or produce overly specific descriptions that fail to capture higher-order, global concepts. We introduce LINE, a novel, training-free iterative approach tailored for open-vocabulary concept labeling in vision models. Operating in a strictly gray-box setting, LINE leverages a large language model and a text-to-image generator to iteratively propose and refine concepts in a closed loop, guided by activation history. We demonstrate that LINE achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple model architectures, yielding AUC improvements of up to 0.15 on ImageNet and 0.05 on Places365, while discovering, on average, 25% of new concepts missed by predefined vocabularies. Beyond identifying the top concept, LINE provides a complete generation history, enabling polysemanticity evaluation and producing supporting visual explanations that rival gradient-dependent activation maximization methods. The LINE source code is available at https://github.com/CredibleAI/LINE

item.title: CitySTAR: Structured and Topology-Aware Reasoning for Open-Vocabulary Urban 3D Grounding
item.description:
Relevance: 27% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Shuai Zhang, Hongye Hou, Qinghe Liu, Zhuoxiao Li, Dongli Wu, Jing Ou, Yuan Liu, Wufan Zhao
arXiv:2609.19911v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: 3D grounding aims to localize target entities in complex scenes from natural language and plays a fundamental role in embodied perception and spatial reasoning. However, existing approaches mostly rely on feature similarity or direct matching, making it difficult to connect natural-language intent with the implicit semantic and geometric structures hidden in billion-scale urban point clouds. We reformulate city-scale 3D grounding as structured constraint reasoning, where description semantics are organized into computable cross-modal constraints over open-vocabulary 3D entities, attributes, and spatial relations. We present CitySTAR, a training-free framework for reasoning-driven urban 3D grounding. CitySTAR lifts raw billion-scale urban point clouds into a query-ready scene graph of open-vocabulary 3D instances, with CodeLLM-driven tools supplying multimodal evidence for node attributes and 3D spatial relations. It then models target-context topology with paired hypergraphs and performs bidirectional topology verification for structural disambiguation. Finally, a Reflective Cross-modal Grounding module integrates topology consistency and candidate-centered 2D visual evidence to make decisions over a metric-aware 3D context graph. To further support this setting, we introduce CitySTAR-3D, an enhanced benchmark that improves semantic coverage, instance completeness, bounding-box fidelity, and spatial-relation complexity in city-scale 3D grounding. Extensive experiments show that CitySTAR consistently improves open-world urban 3D grounding while maintaining strong interpretability and generalization.

item.title: Scaling Optimization-Oriented Hypernetworks for Implicit Neural Representations
item.description:
Relevance: 27% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Lulu Cai, Hanxiang Ren, Siyan Dong, Li Sun, Jiefeng Wu, Youyi Zheng, Yi Ma, Yanchao Yang
arXiv:2611.10509v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a hypernetwork that generates the parameters of an implicit neural representation (INR) for a given signal in a single forward pass, without test-time optimization. Existing hypernetworks for this problem either ignore the chain-rule structure of the test-time optimization that produces an INR or, when they preserve it, instantiate the structure with MLPs whose parameter count grows quartically in target-network width. Our central contribution is to show that this parameter-count cost is structural to the MLP instantiation, not to the optimization-oriented principle of preserving chain-rule structure, and to resolve it by replacing the MLP body with attention. The resulting hypernetwork combines three design choices: an output-neuron-centric tokenization that aligns the token axis with each layer's output-neuron axis; an information-flow consistency rule that fixes the role of every cross-attention module from the representation its output should occupy; and a token-space iterative rollout that realizes the five quantities one optimization step on the target INR computes as five cross-attention modules with parameter count independent of target-network width. Across five 2D and 3D INR generation benchmarks, our method outperforms the state-of-the-art single-pass and optimization-oriented baselines; scales to target-network widths at which the MLP-based optimization-oriented paradigm exhausts GPU memory; and produces the highest result on NeRF generation without ground-truth INR weights supervision.

item.title: Read It Back: Pretrained MLLMs Are Zero-Shot Reward Models for Text-to-Image Generation
item.description:
Relevance: 27% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Runhui Huang, Qihui Zhang, Zhe Liu, Yu Gao, Jie Wu, Hengshuang Zhao
arXiv:2607.11886v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this paper, we propose SpectraReward, a training-free reward function that turns pretrained MLLMs into off-the-shelf reward models for image-generation reinforcement learning. Instead of asking the MLLM to judge a generated image or answer decomposed verification questions, SpectraReward measures how well the original prompt can be recovered from the generated image through a single image-conditioned, teacher-forced forward pass. We use the average image-conditioned prompt log-likelihood as the reward, directly reusing the MLLM's pretrained image-text alignment ability without preference labels, reward-model fine-tuning. We further introduce Self-SpectraReward, a special case for unified multimodal models where the policy's own understanding branch serves as the reward model for its generation branch, forming a closed-loop self-improving framework without external reward models or external knowledge. Extensive experiments validate SpectraReward through a broad image-generation RL study covering two diffusion models, three RL algorithms, nine reward MLLM backbones from four MLLM families spanning 4B to 235B parameters, and five out-of-distribution text-to-image benchmarks. Results show that both SpectraReward and Self-SpectraReward significantly and consistently improve generation performance and outperform prior MLLM-derived reward training methods. Further analysis reveals that larger reward MLLMs are not always better, while Self-SpectraReward can match or surpass much larger external reward models, suggesting that reward-policy alignment is a key factor for effective image-generation RL. Project Page: https://huangrh99.github.io/SpectraReward/

item.title: Task-Critical Part Alignment Improves Imitation of Object Interactions
item.description:
Relevance: 27% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Denis Hadjivelichkov, Sebastian {\AE}gidius, Valerio Modugno, Dimitrios Kanoulas
arXiv:2611.10664v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This paper presents enhancements to the DINOBot framework for imitation learning of object-object interactions. We introduce two key contributions aimed at improving the accuracy and efficiency of alignment in imitation-based robotic tasks. First, we integrate RANdom SAmple Consensus (RANSAC) for outlier rejection during the alignment phase, effectively mitigating the impact of noisy depth data and spurious feature matches. This improves robustness when transferring demonstrations to real-world applications. Second, we refine the semantic correspondence process by focusing on task-relevant interaction regions, ensuring that the learned representation prioritizes critical object features that influence successful manipulation. We evaluated our approach in a range of real-world manipulation tasks, including picking, insertion, shaking, and pouring, using a robotic system. The experimental results demonstrate an overall improvement of 13.8% in task success rates compared to the baseline, along with faster convergence in the alignment process. These results highlight the effectiveness of our enhancements in improving precision and efficiency for object-object interaction imitation in robotics.

item.title: SplatLab: Autonomous Scientific Discovery for 3DGS Research
item.description:
Relevance: 26% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Seemandhar Jain, Manmohan Chandraker
arXiv:2610.30468v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Reproducing a published 3DGS paper takes weeks of expert engineering before any extension can be proposed. Prior autonomous-research systems read papers, draft hypotheses, and write code, but are limited by short fixed templates, low executability, and weak traceability, and none has been demonstrated end-to-end in a live computer-vision subfield with intense activity. SplatLab is an autonomous research system for 3D Gaussian Splatting that addresses these limitations. Given a research prompt, a target-paper URL, or no input at all, it reproduces a published baseline, proposes an extension, trains and ablates across Mip-NeRF 360 and LLFF, writes the manuscript, and binds every reported number to a logged training run. Five design choices distinguish it: (i) candidates mutate plugins from a verified-reproduction backbone matched to published baselines; (ii) a cascade-weighted Elo tournament across eight islands scores candidates on measured GPU PSNR with verbal-gradient feedback; (iii) a standing falsifier subtracts Elo on failure, integrating stress-test survival into selection; (iv) every reported number is bound to a logged training run, and the run cannot terminate while any claim is unbacked; (v) a seven-category 3DGS taxonomy wraps EVOLVE-BLOCK markers in domain-aligned scaffolds transferable across 3DGS repositories. On PSNR-targeted runs, SplatLab's manuscripts beat their reproduced targets by +0.18 to +3.78 dB, including +3.78 dB on astrophotographic nebula rendering, for which no prior 3DGS method exists. The research cycle compresses from months of graduate-student time to days of mostly autonomous compute. Code, all manuscripts, experiment ledgers, and the cross-run paper store are available on the project page.

item.title: EgoGeneralist: Unifying Egocentric Action-Video Tasks through Video-Native Modeling
item.description:
Relevance: 26% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Yanlin Jin, Bowen Yang, Cheng Zhang, Yifan Yang, Zhe Li, Jianfei Cai, Kai Zhu
arXiv:2611.08477v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Modern video models possess strong visual priors, yet do not natively represent human action in metric 3D space. We present EgoGeneralist, which adapts pretrained video generators to unify action-conditioned video generation, pose estimation, and joint action-video generation for egocentric manipulation. Our role-adaptive action renderer provides video-native representations for multidirectional action-video learning, making metric motion usable as both a spatial control signal and a recoverable generation target. Cross-stream action-video coupling establishes close correspondence between metric motion and visual dynamics through lightweight adaptation while preserving the pretrained visual prior. Together, these designs establish a generalist framework spanning six action-video tasks. With only narrow-domain data, EgoGeneralist generalizes to diverse unseen scenes and interactions with effective action control and visual quality, bridging pretrained visual knowledge and metric 3D human motion.

item.title: QCC-WM: Linking Macro-State Dynamics and Visual Generation via Quotient Causal Construction
item.description:
Relevance: 26% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Zhizhong Fu, Wei Zhou, Zhaoyang Jiang, Yudong Lin, Songlun Li, Zhi Li, Feifan Chen, Gaoming Li, Xiaorong Ding, Yifan Chen
arXiv:2611.12353v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A key challenge in action-conditioned world modeling is to construct macro-states from high-dimensional observations that support recursive prediction under actions, while keeping their predicted evolution consistent with visual changes in generated observations. We propose QCC-WM, a visual world model based on Quotient-based Causal Construction. QCC-WM uses action responses to guide macro-variable construction for recursive action-conditioned prediction. A shared reference quotient measurement constrains the consistency between predicted states and observed changes, allowing macro-level predictions to provide structured constraints for future visual generation. Using translational and rotational actions and their predicted responses, the model aggregates local visual features into macro-nodes with spatial correspondence through causal abstraction, and recursively predicts node content and motion under a shared reference measurement. Macro-level predictions guide future observation generation, while predicted motion transports historical appearance information. Node-level errors between generated observations and macro-level targets are then mapped back to the corresponding spatial regions for correction, improving consistency between visual generation and macro-level predictions. On the US-VLA dataset, QCC-WM achieves an ROI-MSE of 0.01861 for four-step prediction. Compared with the best baseline at each prediction horizon, it reduces LPIPS by 48.59%, 41.68%, and 30.23% for four-step prediction and eight- and sixteen-step recursive extrapolation, respectively. Ablation studies and mechanism analyses show that motion-guided reference transport mainly improves pixel reconstruction, while node-level error feedback further improves perceptual quality and consistency between generated observations and macro-level predictions.

item.title: DeformMaster: An Interactive Physics-Neural World Model for Deformable Objects from Videos
item.description:
Relevance: 26% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Can Li, Zhoujian Li, Ren Li, Jie Gu, Lei Lei, Jingmin Chen, Lei Sun
arXiv:2605.09586v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: World models for deformable objects should recover not only geometry and appearance, but also underlying physical dynamics, interaction grounding, and material behavior. Learning such a model from real videos is challenging because deformable linear, planar, and volumetric objects evolve under high-dimensional deformation, noisy interactions, and complex material response. The model must infer a physical state from visual observations, roll it forward under new interactions, and render the resulting dynamics with high visual fidelity. We therefore present DeformMaster, a video-derived interactive physics-neural world model that turns real interaction videos into an online interactive model of deformable objects within a unified dynamics-and-appearance framework. DeformMaster preserves structured physical rollout while using a neural residual to compensate for unmodeled effects, grounds sparse hand motion as distributed compliant actuators for hand-continuum interaction, represents material response with spatially varying constitutive experts, and drives high-fidelity 4D appearance from the predicted physical evolution. Experiments on real-world deformable-object sequences demonstrate DeformMaster's ability to roll out future dynamics and render dynamic appearance, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines while supporting novel action rollout, material-parameter variation, and dynamic novel-view synthesis. Code and video demos are available at the project page: https://can-lee.github.io/deformmaster-web/

item.title: Video-FLAIR: Not Whether to Reason, But How
item.description:
Relevance: 26% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Yogesh Kulkarni, Pooyan Fazli
arXiv:2608.26495v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Multimodal queries can require different types of reasoning. Some can be answered via perceptual reasoning, extracting information directly from the visual signal, while others require compositional reasoning that combines observations or deliberative reasoning that evaluates competing hypotheses. However, many existing methods apply a uniform reasoning strategy across queries, leading to unnecessary computation on simple tasks and insufficient reasoning on complex ones. We introduce Video-FLAIR, a training framework that learns to select the appropriate reasoning mode for each query using reinforcement learning. During training, the model generates responses under all three modes for the same prompt, enabling direct comparison. A composite reward compares these responses to favor the most effective one based on correctness, grounding, and cost, while discouraging unsupported or misaligned deliberation. This yields a supervision signal for learning adaptive reasoning without per-query annotations. Video-FLAIR improves accuracy over the Qwen2.5-VL base model by +5.4 on MathVista, +4.8 on Video-Holmes, and +4.8 on Video-MMMU, while reducing average token usage to 95 compared to 417 for always-thinking baselines.
